text: Enhancing Li cycling coulombic efficiency while mitigating ‘‘shuttle effect” of Li-S battery through sustained release of LiNO3 Qi Jin a,⇑, Kaixin Zhao a, Lili Wu a, Lu Li a, Long Kong b,⇑, Xitian Zhang a,⇑ a Key Laboratory for Photonic and Electronic Bandgap Materials, Ministry of Education, School of Physics and Electronic Engineering, Harbin Normal University, Harbin 150025, Heilongjiang, China b Frontiers Science Center for Flexible Electronics and Xi’an Institute of Flexible Electronics (IFE), Northwestern Polytechnical University, Xi’an 710129, Shaanxi, China a r t i c l e i n f o Article history: Received 3 May 2023 Revised 20 May 2023 Accepted 21 May 2023 Available online 29 May 2023 Keywords: Lithium-sulfur battery Solid electrolyte interphase LiNO3 Coulombic efficiency Shuttle effect a b s t r a c t In practical lithium-sulfur batteries (LSBs), the shuttle effect and Li cycling coulombic efficiency (CE) are strongly affected by the physicochemical properties of solid electrolyte interphase (SEI).

LiNO3 is widely used as an additive in electrolytes to build a high-quality SEI, but its self-sacrificial nature limits the ability to mitigate the shuttle effect and stabilize Li anode during long-term cycling.

To counteract LiNO3 consumption during long-term cycling without using a high initial concentration, inspired by sustainedrelease drugs, we encapsulated LiNO3 in lithiated Nafion polymer and added an electrolyte co-solvent (1,1,2,2-tetrafluoroethylene 2,2,2-trifluoromethyl ether) with poor LiNO3 solubility to construct highquality and durable F- and N-rich SEI.

Theoretical calculations, experiments, multiphysics simulations, and in-situ observations confirmed that the F- and N-rich SEI can modulate lithium deposition behavior and allow persistent repair of SEI during prolonged cycling.
Hence, the F- and N-rich SEI improves the Li anode cycling CE to 99.63% and alleviates the shuttle effect during long-term cycling.
The lithium anode with sustainable F- and N-rich SEI shows a stable Li plating/stripping over 2000 h at 1 mA cm2.
As expected, Li||S full cells with this SEI achieved a long lifespan of 250 cycles, far exceeding cells with a routine SEI.
The Li||S pouch cell based on F- and N-rich SEI also can achieve a high energy density of about 300 Wh kg1 at initial cycles.

This strategy provides a novel design for high-quality and durable SEIs in LSBs and may also be extendable to other alkali metal batteries.  2023 Science Press and Dalian Institute of Chemical Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences.

Introduction The growing demand for electric vehicles has driven the development of high energy-density secondary battery systems.
The lithium-sulfur battery (LSB) is a promising rechargeable battery owing to its high theoretical specific energy of 2570 Wh kg1 [1,2].
Nonetheless, the low Li cycling efficiency and shuttle effect of lithium polysulfides (LiPSs) lead to quick failure of LSBs and preclude their commercialization [3,4].
These problems are closely linked to an unstable routine solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) [5,6].
Firstly, the shuttle effect originates from long-chain LiPSs dissolved in the electrolyte, which will pass through the routine SEI and react with the metallic Li anode [7,8].
Secondly, the routine SEI with low Li+ conductivity and poor electrical insulation leads to formation of Li dendrite, and thus lowers Li cycling coulombic efficiency (CE) [9,10].
Therefore, regulating the properties of SEI is essential for inhibiting the shuttle effect and improving Li cycling CE.
The properties of an SEI are determined by its components and structure [11,12].
Recently, extensive efforts have been devoted to constructing high-quality SEIs, mainly by tailoring the electrolyte composition or preparing artificial SEIs [13,14].

Among these, additives in the electrolyte such as benzoselenol [15], cerium nitrate [16], 3,5-bis(trifluoromethyl)thiophenol [17], and LiNO3 [18] have been proven to be a facile and effective strategy for optimizing the components and structure of SEI.
Today, LiNO3 is regarded as a superstar additive in the field of LSBs, because a small amount of NO3  can generate a dense SEI enriched with high Li+ conductivity LiNxOy and Li3N components [19–21].

Such a compact SEI strongly mitigates the shuttle effect by preventing the LiPSs from contacting with the Li anode, while a high Li+ conductivity N-rich https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jechem.2023.05.020 2095-4956/ 2023 Science Press and Dalian Institute of Chemical Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences.

SEI can inhibit the formation of Li dendrites, enhancing Li cycling CE [22,23].

A certain amount of LiNO3 can be dissolved in the standard ether-based electrolytes used in LSBs [24], but this additive is gradually depleted during the constant rupture and reconstruction of the SEI.
Once NO3  is exhausted, the electrochemical performance of LSBs deteriorates rapidly in terms of CE and discharge capacity.
The rate of LiNO3 depletion is related to its original amount in the electrolyte and the battery cycling capacity.
Under mild conditions (e.g., at a low S loading and a high electrolyte/sulfur (E/S) ratio), LiNO3 can significantly enhance the lifespan and stability of LSBs [25].
However, a practical LSBs requires the use of a high S loading cathode (>6 mg cm2), lean electrolyte (<3 lL mgS 1), and a thin Li anode (<50 lm) [26].
Under such harsh conditions, even a high concentration of electrolyte failed to achieve satisfactory LSB cycling performance due to premature failure of Li anode [7].

Although a higher initial LiNO3 concentration in the electrolyte directly ensures the sustainability and compactness of SEI, a LiNO3 concentration above 0.5 M not only converts the ‘‘active S” in cathode into inactive sulphate but also increases the cost and viscosity of the electrolyte [27].
So far, there has been no report of a sustainable SEI that continuously mitigates the shuttle effect and enhances the Li cycling CE for practical LSBs.

Researchers recently identified various slow-release strategies for LiNO3 to achieve sustainable SEI in ester-based electrolytes (low LiNO3 solubility), including pre-impregnation of the separator, encapsulation in a polymer gel [28], intercalation between bilayers of the separator [29], and encapsulation in nano capsules [30].
However, these strategies are not applied to LSB electrolytes because of the high solubility of LiNO3 in 1,3-dioxolane (DOL) and dimethoxy ethane (DME) [31].
In the drug field, reducing the drug release rate is a common means of improving the effectiveness of the drug [32,33].

Compared to conventional methods, drugs in sustained release systems can maintain effective concentrations for longer periods of time, prolong the duration of action, increase the effectiveness, and improve the utilisation of the drug [34,35].
Herein, inspired by sustained-release drugs strategies, we encapsulated LiNO3 in polymers and added ether-based cosolvent for solubility-mediated sustained release during LSB cycling.
The goal of this strategy is to construct a high-quality and durable SEI to mitigate the shuttle effect and improve the CE of Li plating/stripping.
Specifically, the LiNO3 nanoparticles were dispersed in lithiated Nafion (Li-Nafion) polymer and coated on a polypropylene melt-blown cloth.
This LiNO3 sustained-release film (LNO-SRF) swells in the electrolyte to achieve sustained release of LiNO3.

At the same time, a fluorinated ether with ultralow Li salts solubility (1,1,2,2-tetrafluoroethylene 2,2,2-trifluoromethyl ether, TFTFE) was added to the electrolyte as a co-solvent to further slow down the release of LiNO3 and generate insulating LiF component in the SEI, inhibiting electron leakage.

During battery operation, a high-quality and durable SEI enriched with F and N was formed, and it increased the Li plating/stripping CE to 99.63% at a current of 1.0 mA cm2, a capacity of 1.0 mA h cm2.

In a Li||S full cell with a high S loading cathode, a low E/S ratio, and a limited excess Li anode, the shuttle effect of LiPSs was effectively suppressed during cycling and an outstanding cycling lifespan of 250 cycles was achieved. 2.
Fabrication of LNO-SRF Li-Nafion powder was prepared according to previous reports [36].
LiNO3 (10 wt%) and Li-Nafion (1 wt%) powder were fully dissolved in N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP) under magnetic stirring.
The mixed solution was blade-coated onto a polypropylene meltblown cloth and dried in a vacuum oven at 80 C.
The obtained LNO-SRF was punched into 15-mm round disks and transferred to a glovebox.
The mass of LNO-SRF is about 3 mg cm2, and the LiNO3 loading is about 1.2 mg cm2.
The LNO-SRF was placed between separator and Li electrode or Cu electrode. 2.2.
Electrochemical measurements All electrochemical tests were performed in CR2032-type coin cells with Celgard 2400 separators.
Three types of cells (symmetric Li||Li, Li||Cu, and Li||S) were assembled in a glovebox.
Electrochemical tests were conducted using an electrochemical workstation (BioLogic, France) and a LAND battery test system.
Details of the electrochemical tests are described in the Supporting Information. 2.3.

Calculations and multiphysics simulation Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were carried out using the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP) to obtain the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) and electrostatic potential (ESP) charge distributions of various solvents and anions.
Finite element modelling (FEM) was conducted using COMSOL multiphysics software.
Details of the computation and simulation are provided in Supporting Information. 3.

Results and discussion To construct a high-quality and sustainable SEI in LSBs, we propose using Li-Nafion to encapsulate LiNO3 nanoparticles and adding 10 vt% TFTFE as a co-solvent to the electrolyte.
The freestanding LNO-SRF was prepared by blade-coating a mixture of LiNO3 and Li-Nafion in NMP on a polypropylene melt-blown cloth (Fig. 1a).
The as-prepared LNO-SRF was characterized using X-ray diffractometer (XRD) (Fig. 1b).
The crystalline peak of 2h  18 is related to the Li-Nafion [37], and other crystalline peaks are assigned to LiNO3.

In contrast to the smooth surface of uncoated cloth fibres, the scanning electron microscopy (SEM) image of the LNO-SRF fibres revealed some surface sediments, proving that Li-Nafion/LiNO3 was evenly coated on the polypropylene fibres (Fig. 1c and d).
S1, the thickness of LNO-SRF is about 140 lm.
In addition, the contact angle between the LNO-SRF and electrolyte was only 25 (Fig. 1e).
The homogeneous dispersion of LiNO3 nanoparticles and the small contact angle facilitate LNO-SRF wetting by the electrolyte and continuous release of LiNO3 during battery operation.
Moreover, the LiNO3 has a low solubility in TFTFE, as evidenced by the obvious sediments formed at the bottom of TFTFE after adding only 0.01 M LiNO3 (Fig.
Therefore, TFTFE as a co-solvent should slow the release of LiNO3 in the electrolyte.

To investigate the effects of LNO-SRF and TFTFE co-solvent on the speed of LiNO3 release, after soaking LNO-SRF in different electrolytes (1 M LiTFSI-DOL/DME or 1 M LiTFSI-DOL/DME/TFTFE) for various times (Fig.
S3), the electrolytes were analyzed by inductively coupled plasma-optical emission spectrometry (ICP-OES) and UV-vis absorption spectroscopy.

As shown in Fig. 1(f), the Li element content of 1 M LiTFSI-DOL/DME was 7.14, 7.56, 8.22, 8.82, and 10.05 g L1 after soaking LNO-SRF for 12, 24, 36, 48, and 168 h, respectively, illustrating that NO3  in the electrolyte was continuously replenished from the electrolyte-swelled LNO- SRF.

In contrast, the Li element content of 1 M LiTFSI-DOL/DME/ TFTFE was 7.14, 7.38, 7.56, 8.28, and 9.90 g L1 at the corresponding soaking time, suggesting that the introduction of TFTFE further slowed down LiNO3 release speed.

These results demonstrate that the combined strategy of using Li-Nafionencapsulated LiNO3 and adding TFTFE as a co-solvent helps maintain an appreciable NO3  concentration near the Li anode, allowing LiNO3 to function as a sacrificial additive during the long cycling process of LSBs.
To understand the influence of LNO-SRF and TFTFE on the SEI, the LUMO level of DME, DOL, TFSI, TFTFE, and NO3  was calculated using DFT, and the results are shown in Fig. 2(a).

The NO3  has a much lower LUMO energy (1.27 eV) than that of the other solvents (0.42, 0.38, and 0.17 eV for DME, DOL, and TFTFE, respectively) and TFSI (0.08 eV), indicating that NO3  can be easily reduced on the Li anode surface to form an N-rich SEI.
Notably, the LUMO energy of TFTFE is also lower than DME, DOL, and TFSI, implying that the formed SEI should be enriched in F.
Next, we simulated the ESP charge distributions of DME, DOL, TFSI, TFTFE, and NO3  using DFT calculations (Fig. 2b).
The negative charge is concentrated around NO3 , facilitating its coordination with the Li+ and participation in the solvation structure of Li+.
This was confirmed using 7Li nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy.
As shown in Fig. 2(c), a higher LiNO3 content in electrolyte led to a lower 7Li chemical shift due to a shielding effect of the solvation sheath on Li+.
This was induced by the extra NO3 , which interacted more strongly with Li+.
The NO3  will preferentially decompose on the surface of the Li anode accompanied by the desolvation process of Li+.
Therefore, the NO3  concentration at the Li anode surface determines the content of inorganic Li-N components in the SEI (Li3N and LiNxOy).
To verify the above conclusions, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) analysis was performed with continuous etching from the surface to the bottom of SEIs formed in Li||Li cells.

A total of four cell configurations were examined: with neither LNO-SRF nor TFTFE (denoted by R-SEI), without LNO-SRF but with TFTFE (denoted by F-SEI), with LNO-SRF but not TFTFE (denoted by N- SEI), and with both LNO-SRF and TFTFE (denoted by FN-SEI).
First, the concentration of C atoms in different SEIs was measured as an indicator of the organic components.

S4, the C atomic ratios in R-SEI, F-SEI, N-SEI, and FN-SEI surfaces were 24.45%, 16.91%, 12.28%, and 10.73%, respectively, suggesting that the LNO-SRT and TFTFE co-solvent together can significantly increase the content of inorganic species in SEI.

A higher inorganic content means a more compact SEI with enhanced mechanical properties, ionic conductivity, and insulation; all of them can inhibit shuttle effect and increase the CE of Li cycling [39].
Second, the F 1s and N 1s XPS spectra were analyzed to clarify the effects of LNO-SRF and TFTFE co-solvent on the SEI components and structure.
In the F 1s spectra of R-SEI, F-SEI, N-SEI, and FN-SEI at different etching times (Fig. 2d), two peaks related to –CF3 and LiF were detected at both 0 and 400 s.
It is worth noting that the intensities of two peaks were significantly higher in F-SEI and FN-SEI compared to those in R-SEI and N-SEI, due to the use of TFTFE as a co-solvent.

Generally, the chemical composition of SEI significantly influences the nucleation and growth of Li.
Therefore, the morphology and surface flatness of Li deposited below various SEIs were analyzed.
For R-SEI, the Li electrode surface displayed a loose, uneven, and dendritic surface, and greyish-black dead Li was observed after only five cycles in Li||Li cell (Fig. 3a).
A porous and loose structure of deposited Li will exacerbate the side reactions on the surface of Li electrode, resulting in massive Li dendrites and shuttle effect.

When the content of LiF (F-SEI) or Li3N/LiNxOy (N-SEI) components in the SEI increases, Li deposition became more uniform, with somewhat inhibited growth of Li dendrites and dead Li formation (Fig. 3b and c).

In contrast, the surface of Li electrode with FN-SEI was quite dense and smooth without obvious dendrites or dead Li (Fig. 3d), indicating that the F- and N-rich SEI could effectively regulate Li+ deposition and suppress dendritic growth.
In addition, FN-SEI had a high Young’s modulus of 4.95 GPa (Fig.
S6), which inhibited the growth of Li dendrites.
This suppression of Li dendrites significantly reduced the reactive surface area, thus lowering the possibility side reactions.
The average CE is a key index for the cyclability of Li electrodes.
According to the method proposed by Zhang et al.
[41], we determined the average CE of Li stripping/plating in Li||Cu cells with different SEIs.
The time-voltage curves of Li||Cu cells with R-SEI, F-SEI, N-SEI, and FN-SEI are shown in Fig. 3(e–h), respectively.
Among them, the cell with FN-SEI displayed the lowest nucleation overpotential of 46 mV and deposit overpotential of 24 mV (Fig.
S7), suggesting that FN-SEI has the highest Li+ conductivity, which is in line with the electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) measurements (Fig.
In addition, the cell with FN-SEI had the highest CE of 99.63%, exceeding those cells with R-SEI (98.46%), F-SEI (99.02%), and N-SEI (99.17%).

To understand the reasons behind this high CE and small polarization of the cell with FN-SEI, the exchange current density (i0) was obtained by fitting the Tafel plots of the Li||Li cells with various SEIs.
The i0 value of FN-SEI cell reaches 1.58 mA cm2, which is 7.2, 2.8, and 1.7 times larger than that of R-SEI, F-SEI, and N- SEI cells (0.22, 0.56, and 0.91 mA cm2, respectively; Fig. 4a).

FN-SEI exhibited a smaller activation energy (4.46 kJ mol1) than R-SEI (9.06 kJ mol1), F-SEI (7.17 kJ mol1), and N-SEI (6.02 kJ mol1) (Fig. 4b).
The high exchange current density and low activation energy indicate that FN-SEI has a strong ability for Li+ transport.
Next, the Li||Cu and Li||Li cells with different SEIs were cycled to study the cycling stability of their Li electrodes.
The Li||Li cell (using 100 lm Li electrode) with FN-SEI achieved stable and long-lasting cycling performance (up to 2000 h) without short circuits (Fig.
S9), much longer than that of the Li||Li cell with R-SEI (560 h), F-SEI (1054 h), and N-SEI (1400 h) (Fig. 4c).
It is worth noting that the independent use of Li-Nafion membrane also reduce the polarization of Li plating/stripping process to a certain extent (Fig.
The Li||Cu cell with FN-SEI also showed a high stability over 400 cycles, while the CE for R-SEI, F-SEI, and N-SEI decayed rapidly within 25, 98, and 135 cycles, respectively (Fig. 4d).

The main reason for fast CE fading in these cells is that R-SEI, F-SEI, and N-SEI cannot effectively suppress the growth of Li dendrites with a large surface area, leading to non-negligible side reactions and excess ‘‘dead Li” formed in each plating/stripping cycle.
In contrast, the higher content of LiF, Li3N, and LiNxOy in FN-SEI strongly favours homogeneous Li deposition.
Meanwhile, LNO-SRF can replenish LiNO3 consumed in the electrolyte during cycling.

The in-situ optical microscopy (OM) images show that FN-SEI ensured a dense structure of Li anode during continuous Li deposition.
As shown in Fig. 4(e), in-situ cells based on a standard electrolyte began to exhibit obviously Li dendrites after 30 min discharge, and by 60 min the Li dendrites had become very loose.
Conversely, no Li dendrites were observed in the in-situ cell with FN-SEI.
Fig. 4(f) shows Li deposition morphology on the in-suit cells.
A loose and dendritic surface was observed on the Li electrode with R-SEI, while that with FN-SEI exhibited spherical deposited Li with a dense and smooth surface instead of dendrites.
Based on the distinct Li plating morphologies observed experimentally, we simulated the current density distributions, as shown in Fig. 4(g).
The flat surface of plated Li resulted in a uniform current distribution, suppressing the needle-like growth of Li.

To prove that durable N- and F-rich SEI can prolong LSB life, coin-type Li||S full cells with R-SEI and FN-SEI were assembled.
Notably, a low negative-to-positive capacity (N/P) ratio and E/S ratio are important for practical LSBs.

Hence, we employed a commercial-level carbon nanotubes/sulfur cathode (S loading: 5 mg cm2, 8.36 mA h cm2), a limited amount of Li (50 lm, 10 mA h cm2) with an N/P ratio of around 1.2, and lean electrolyte (5 lL mgS 1).

First, the shuttle current was measured in cells with R-SEI and FN-SEI at initial cycles and 25 cycles to demonstrate that FN-SEI could effectively suppress the shuttle effect during long-term cycling.
As shown in Fig. 5(a and b), the shuttle currents of these two cells were not significantly different in the initial cycle, and both were close to 0.
However, after 25 cycles the shuttle current of the FN-SEI cell was approximately five times lower than that of the R-SEI cell, indicating that FN-SEI maintained a dense state during cycling.
S14, Li||S cells with R-SEI and FN-SEI exhibited nearly identical initial discharge capacities of about 1250 mA h g1.
After approximately 25 cycles, the discharge capacity for R-SEI decreased rapidly with concurrent dramatic fluctuations in CE because of severe dendrite growth and exhaustion of LiNO3.
In contrast, Li||S cell with FN-SEI exhibited stable cycling over 250 cycles (Fig. 5c).
The degradation discrepancy between cells can be explained by the charge-discharge profiles.
The polarization voltage of the Li||S cell with R-SEI rapidly increased to 360 mV, whereas that of the Li||S cell with FN-SEI was only 220 mV (Fig.
This is ascribed to severe passivation of R-SEI, which causes increase of polarization.

The structure and chemical components of the cycled Li anode surface were further analyzed by XPS.
Based on the S 2p spectra (Fig. 5d and e), strong peaks of Li2S and Li2SOx were observed on the Li anode with R-SEI, whereas Li anode with FN-SEI exhibited much weaker Li2S and Li2SOx peaks.
The smaller amounts of S-containing species can be attributed to fewer side reactions occurring between Li anode and LiPSs.
The assembled Li||S cell with FN-SEI was further used to power electronic devices to validate their practical applications.

As shown in Fig. 5 (g), the Li||S pouch cell can light diode, driving the fan and charging the mobile phone.

After 20 cycles, the pouch cell with FN-SEI delivers a high reversible capacity of 1.55 Ah (Fig.

More impressively, the energy density of Li||S pouch cell with FN-SEI is about 300 Wh kg1 at initial cycles (based on the mass of the whole cell), which exhibits great potential for practical applications.

As shown in Fig. 5(h), benefiting from the fact that FN-SEI can shield LiPSs, accelerate Li+ transfer, and suppress electron tunneling, thus improving the CE of Li anodes, and suppressing the shuttle effect in actual LSBs, LSBs containing FN-SEI have such excellent electrochemical properties. 4.

Conclusions In summary, to enhance the cycling life of Li anodes and promote further practical applications of LSBs, we designed and constructed a high-quality and durable F- and N-rich SEI on the Li anode by utilizing LNO-SRF and TFTFE as co-solvents in the electrolyte.
LNO-SRF provided a continuous release of LiNO3 into the electrolyte, and the TFTFE co-solvent slowed the release speed of LiNO3, resulting in a dense and durable F- and N-rich SEI.
The formation mechanism of such a superior SEI was determined using DFT calculations.
Such an SEI effectively suppresses Li dendrite formation and regulates Li deposition, as demonstrated by the experimental results.

This combined strategy for continuous LiNO3 release may provide new guidelines for developing advanced LSBs.

Supporting Information Enhancing Li Cycling Coulombic Efficiency While Mitigating “Shuttle Effect” of Li–S Battery Through Sustained Release of LiNO3 Experimental Section Battery Assembly and Electrochemical Measurements: The standard electrolyte of LSBs is composed of 1 M lithium bis (trifluoromethane sulfonyl) imide (LiTFSI) in 1, 3-dioxolane (DOL)/1, 2-dimethoxyethane (DME) with a volume ratio of 1:1, and 2 wt% LiNO3.
The fluorinated electrolyte is composed of 1 M LiTFSI in DOL/DME/TFTFE with a volume ratio of 4.5:4.5:1, and 2 wt% LiNO3.

A total of four cell configurations were examined: with neither LNO-SRF nor TFTFE (denoted by R-SEI), without LNO-SRF but with TFTFE (denoted by F-SEI), with LNO-SRF but not TFTFE (denoted by N-SEI), and with both LNO-SRF and TFTFE (denoted by FN-SEI).
For Li||Li symmetrical cells, bare Li electrodes (thickness: 50 μm) were used as the working and counter electrode.
The amount of standard or fluorinated electrolyte was 40 μL in each cell.
For Li||Cu cells, Cu foil electrodes were used as the working electrode, and Li foil were used as counter electrode.
The amount of standard or fluorinated electrolyte also was 40 μL in each cell.
The Li plating/stripping tests were performed on the LAND CT3001A (Wuhan, China) battery test system at a current density of 1 mA cm–2 with a capacity of 1 mAh cm–2, respectively.
The cyclic voltammetry (CV) curves of Li||Li cell were tested on an electrochemical station with the potential ranging from -0.2 to 0.2 V at a scan rate of 0.1 mV s−1.
The exchange current density of the electrode was obtained from the CV data.
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) measurements were conducted using an electrochemical workstation within a frequency range of 10 mHz-100 kHz under a voltage amplitude of 10 mV.
The activation energy for Li+ through various SEI was obtained via EIS tests at different temperatures.
At each temperature, the Li||Li cell was equilibrated for 60 min before the measurement.
The Li plating/stripping CEs were tested in Li||Cu cells at a current density of 1 mA cm−2, capacity of 1 mAh cm−2.
For Li||S full cells, CNT/S cathodes (S loading 5.0 mg cm−2) were prepared according to previous reports.

Specifically, 80 wt% CNT/S powders, 10 wt% Super P, and 10 wt% polyvinylidene difluorides were mixed in NMP The slurry was coated onto aluminium foils and dried in a vacuum drying oven at 60oC for 12 h.
The CNT/S electrodes were used as cathodes, and bare Li electrodes (thickness: 50 μm) were used as anodes.
The galvanostatic measurements of the Li||S cells were conducted on LAND systems in a voltage range of 1.7-2.6 V.
Shuttle currents of the Li||S cells with R-SEI and FN-SEI were measured.

Before the shuttle current test, the cell was galvanostatically charged and discharged at 0.1 C for different cycles, and then the cells were galvanostatically charged to the 100 % state at 2.9 V, followed by discharging to different voltage stages at 2.90, 2.60, 2.45, 2.43, 2.40, 2.39, 2.38, 2.37, 2.36, 2.35, 2.34, 2.25, and 2.20 V, and then switched to potentiostatic mode.
The shuttle current was a potentiostatic steady-state current at different voltage levels.
